title: Chapter 27
paragraphs: Sometime in the afternoon I raised my head, and looking around and seeing the western sun casting the sign of its decline on the wall, I asked myself, "What am I to do?"

But the answer my mind gave—"Leave Thornfield at once"—was so immediate, so terrifying, that I covered my ears. I told myself I could not bear such words right now. "That I am not Edward Rochester's bride is the least part of my grief," I argued. "That I have been woken from the most glorious dreams and found them all empty and meaningless—that is a horror I could bear and overcome. But that I must leave him—decisively, instantly, entirely—is intolerable. I cannot do it."

But then a voice inside me declared that I could do it, and predicted that I would. I wrestled with my own resolution. I wanted to be weak, so I could avoid the dreadful passage of further suffering I saw stretching out before me. And Conscience, turned tyrant, held Passion by the throat, told her mockingly that she had only dipped her dainty foot into the mire, and swore that with his iron arm he would plunge her down to depths of agony beyond measure.
"Let me be torn away, then!" I cried. "Let someone else help me!"

"No. You shall tear yourself away. No one shall help you. You shall pluck out your own right eye. You shall cut off your own right hand. Your heart shall be the victim, and you the priest who pierces it."

I rose up suddenly, terrified by the solitude that so ruthless a judge haunted—by the silence that so awful a voice filled. My head swam as I stood upright. I realized I was growing faint from agitation and hunger; I had eaten and drunk nothing all day, having skipped breakfast. And with a strange pang, I now reflected that, long as I had been shut in here, no one had sent a message to ask how I was or to invite me downstairs. Not even little Adèle had knocked at the door. Not even Mrs. Fairfax had come looking for me. "Friends always forget those whom fortune abandons," I murmured, as I unbolted the door and stepped out. I stumbled over an obstacle—my head was still dizzy, my vision dim, and my limbs feeble. I could not recover myself. I fell, but not to the ground: an outstretched arm caught me. I looked up—I was being held by Mr. Rochester, who sat in a chair across my bedroom threshold.

"You come out at last," he said. "I have been waiting for you a long time, and listening. Yet I heard not a single movement, not a single sob. Five more minutes of that deathlike silence, and I would have forced the lock like a burglar. So you avoid me? You shut yourself away and grieve alone! I would rather you had come and berated me furiously. You are passionate—I expected a scene of some kind. I was prepared for a downpour of tears; I only wanted them shed on my chest. Instead a senseless floor has received them, or your soaked handkerchief. But no—I am wrong: you have not wept at all! I see a white cheek and a faded eye, but no trace of tears. I suppose, then, your heart has been weeping blood?"

"Well, Jane! Not a word of reproach? Nothing bitter—nothing piercing? Nothing to wound a feeling or sting a passion? You sit quietly where I have placed you and look at me with a weary, passive expression."

"Jane, I never meant to wound you like this. If a man who had only one little lamb—dear to him as a daughter, that ate from his plate and drank from his cup and lay in his arms—had by some mistake slaughtered it at the butcher's, he would not have regretted his bloody blunder more than I now regret mine. Will you ever forgive me?"

Reader, I forgave him at that moment and on that spot. There was such deep remorse in his eye, such genuine pity in his tone, such manly energy in his manner. And besides, there was such unchanged love in his whole look and bearing—I forgave him everything. Yet not in words, not outwardly; only at the core of my heart.
"You know I am a scoundrel, Jane?" he asked after a while, wistfully—wondering, I suppose, at my continued silence and tameness, which came from weakness rather than choice.
"Yes, sir."
"Then tell me so bluntly and sharply—don't spare me."

"I cannot. I am tired and sick. I want some water." He let out a sort of shuddering sigh, and taking me in his arms, carried me downstairs. At first I did not know what room he had brought me to; everything was blurred to my glazed sight. Soon I felt the reviving warmth of a fire; for, summer as it was, I had grown ice-cold in my room. He put wine to my lips; I tasted it and revived. Then I ate something he offered me, and was soon myself again. I was in the library—sitting in his chair—he was very close. "If I could leave this life now, without too sharp a pang, it would be well for me," I thought. "Then I would not have to crack my heartstrings in tearing them away from Mr. Rochester. I must leave him, it seems. I do not want to leave him—I cannot leave him."
"How are you now, Jane?"
"Much better, sir. I shall be well soon."
"Taste the wine again, Jane."

I obeyed. Then he put the glass on the table, stood before me, and looked at me closely. Suddenly he turned away with an inarticulate exclamation, full of passionate emotion of some kind. He walked rapidly through the room and came back. He leaned toward me as if to kiss me; but I remembered that such gestures were now forbidden. I turned my face away and pushed his aside.
"What!—How is this?" he exclaimed quickly. "Oh, I know! You won't kiss the husband of Bertha Mason? You consider my arms full and my embraces spoken for?"
"At any rate, there is neither room nor claim for me, sir."
"Why, Jane? I will spare you the trouble of much talking. I will answer for you—Because I already have a wife, you would reply. Am I right?"
"Yes."

"If you think so, you must have a strange opinion of me. You must see me as a scheming scoundrel—a base and low rake who has been pretending to love you selflessly in order to lure you into a trap deliberately set, to strip you of your honor and rob you of your self-respect. What do you say to that? I see you can say nothing. In the first place, you are still faint and have all you can do just to breathe. In the second place, you cannot yet bring yourself to accuse and condemn me. And besides, the floodgates of tears are opening, and they would pour out if you spoke much. You have no desire to argue or reproach or make a scene: you are thinking how to act—talking, you believe, is pointless. I know you—I am on my guard."
"Sir, I do not wish to act against you," I said; and my unsteady voice warned me to cut my words short.

"Not in your sense of the word, but in mine you are plotting to destroy me. You have as good as said that I am a married man—as a married man you will avoid me, keep out of my way. Just now you refused to kiss me. You intend to make yourself a complete stranger to me: to live under this roof only as Adèle's governess. If ever I say a friendly word to you, if ever a friendly feeling draws you to me again, you will say, 'That man nearly made me his mistress: I must be ice and rock to him.' And ice and rock you will become."

I cleared and steadied my voice to reply: "Everything has changed around me, sir. I must change too—there is no doubt of that. And to avoid swings of feeling and constant battles with memories and associations, there is only one way—Adèle must have a new governess, sir."

"Oh, Adèle will go to school—I have already settled that. Nor do I mean to torment you with the hideous associations and memories of Thornfield Hall—this accursed place—this tent of Achan—this vault of insolence, offering the ghastliness of living death to the light of the open sky—this narrow stone hell, with its one real demon, worse than a legion of the kind we imagine. Jane, you shall not stay here, and neither will I. I was wrong ever to bring you to Thornfield Hall, knowing as I did how it was haunted. I ordered them to hide from you, before I ever met you, all knowledge of the curse on this place—simply because I feared Adèle would never keep a governess if the woman knew what fellow resident she shared the house with. And my plans would not let me move the madwoman elsewhere—though I own an old house, Ferndean Manor, even more remote and hidden than this, where I could have housed her safely enough, had not a scruple about the unhealthy location, deep in the woods, made my conscience recoil from the arrangement. Probably those damp walls would soon have relieved me of her. But to each villain his own vice; and mine is not a tendency toward indirect murder, even of what I most hate."

"However, concealing the madwoman's presence from you was something like covering a child with a cloak and laying it near a poison tree: that demon's proximity is toxic, and always was. But I will shut up Thornfield Hall. I will nail up the front door and board the lower windows. I will pay Mrs. Poole two hundred a year to live here with my wife, as you call that fearful creature. Grace will do much for money, and she shall have her son—the keeper at Grimsby Retreat—to bear her company and help her during the fits, when my wife is driven by her demons to burn people in their beds at night, to stab them, to tear the flesh from their bones, and so on—"
"Sir," I interrupted him, "you are merciless toward that unfortunate woman. You speak of her with hatred—with vindictive hostility. It is cruel—she cannot help being mad."

"Jane, my little darling (I will call you that, because you are), you don't know what you are talking about. You misjudge me again: it is not because she is mad that I hate her. If you were mad, do you think I would hate you?"
"I do indeed, sir."

"Then you are mistaken, and you know nothing about me, and nothing about the kind of love I am capable of. Every atom of your body is as dear to me as my own. In pain and sickness it would still be dear. Your mind is my treasure, and if it were shattered, it would be my treasure still. If you raved, my arms should hold you—not a straitjacket. Your grip, even in fury, would have a charm for me. If you flew at me as wildly as that woman did this morning, I would receive you in an embrace at least as tender as it was firm. I would not shrink from you with disgust as I did from her. In your quiet moments you would have no watcher and no nurse but me. I could bend over you with untiring tenderness, though you gave me no smile in return, and never tire of gazing into your eyes, though they no longer held a ray of recognition for me.—But why do I follow that line of thought? I was talking about taking you away from Thornfield. Everything, you know, is ready for an immediate departure. Tomorrow you shall go. I only ask you to endure one more night under this roof, Jane; and then, farewell to its miseries and terrors forever! I have a place to go to that will be a safe refuge from hateful memories, from unwelcome intrusion—even from lies and slander."
"And take Adèle with you, sir," I interrupted. "She will be a companion for you."

"What do you mean, Jane? I told you I would send Adèle to school. And what would I want with a child for a companion—and not my own child, but a French dancer's bastard? Why do you press me about her! I say, why do you suggest Adèle as my companion?"
"You spoke of a retreat, sir; and retreat and solitude are dull. Too dull for you."
"Solitude! Solitude!" he repeated with irritation. "I see I must explain myself. I don't know what sphinx-like expression is forming on your face. You are to share my solitude. Do you understand?"

I shook my head. It took a degree of courage, agitated as he was becoming, even to risk that mute sign of refusal. He had been pacing rapidly around the room, and he stopped, as if suddenly rooted to one spot. He looked at me long and hard. I turned my eyes away from him, fixed them on the fire, and tried to assume and maintain a quiet, composed expression.

"Now for the snag in Jane's character," he said at last, speaking more calmly than his look had led me to expect. "The reel of silk has run smoothly enough so far; but I always knew there would come a knot and a tangle: here it is. Now for frustration, and fury, and endless trouble! By God! I long to use a fraction of Samson's strength and snap the entanglement like string!"
He resumed his pacing, but soon stopped again, this time right in front of me.

"Jane! Will you listen to reason?" (He stooped and brought his lips to my ear.) "Because if you won't, I'll try force." His voice was hoarse; his look that of a man about to snap an unbearable restraint and plunge headlong into wild abandon. I saw that in another moment, with one more surge of frenzy, I would be able to do nothing with him. The present—the passing second—was all I had in which to control and restrain him. A movement of rejection, flight, or fear would have sealed my fate—and his. But I was not afraid. Not in the least. I felt an inner power, a sense of influence, that supported me. The crisis was dangerous, but not without its thrill: like, perhaps, what a man feels when he slips over the rapids in his canoe. I took hold of his clenched fist, loosened the knotted fingers, and said to him soothingly—
"Sit down. I will talk to you as long as you like, and hear everything you have to say, whether reasonable or unreasonable."

He sat down, but he did not get to speak right away. I had been fighting back tears for some time, taking great pains to suppress them because I knew he would not want to see me cry. Now, however, I decided it was better to let them flow as freely and as long as they wished. If the flood annoyed him, so much the better. So I gave in and wept hard.
Soon I heard him earnestly begging me to compose myself. I said I could not while he was in such a state.
"But I am not angry, Jane. I only love you too much. And you had set your little pale face with such a resolute, frozen look—I could not bear it. Hush now, and dry your eyes."
His softened voice told me he was subdued; so I, in turn, became calm. Now he tried to rest his head on my shoulder, but I would not allow it. Then he tried to draw me to him: no.

"Jane! Jane!" he said, in such a tone of bitter sadness that it thrilled through every nerve I had. "You don't love me, then? It was only my position, and the rank of my wife, that you valued? Now that you think I'm not fit to be your husband, you recoil from my touch as if I were some toad or ape."

Those words cut me. Yet what could I do or say? I probably should have done or said nothing; but I was so tormented by guilt at hurting his feelings that I could not resist the urge to soothe where I had wounded.
"I do love you," I said, "more than ever. But I must not show or indulge the feeling. And this is the last time I must express it."
"The last time, Jane! What! Do you think you can live with me, see me every day, and yet, if you still love me, be always cold and distant?"
"No, sir. That I am certain I could not. And so I see there is only one way: but you will be furious if I say it."
"Oh, say it! If I rage, you have the art of weeping."
"Mr. Rochester, I must leave you."
"For how long, Jane? For a few minutes, while you smooth your hair—which is somewhat disheveled—and bathe your face—which looks feverish?"
"I must leave Adèle and Thornfield. I must part from you for my whole life. I must begin a new existence among strange faces and strange scenes."

"Of course: I told you that you would. I'll skip over the madness about parting from me. You mean you must become a part of me. As for the new existence, it's exactly right: you shall still be my wife. I am not married. You shall be Mrs. Rochester—both in reality and in name. I shall be faithful only to you for as long as we both live. You shall go to a place I have in the south of France: a whitewashed villa on the shores of the Mediterranean. There you shall live a happy, protected, and perfectly innocent life. Never fear that I wish to lure you into sin—to make you my mistress. Why did you shake your head? Jane, you must be reasonable, or I swear I shall go mad again."
His voice and hand trembled. His nostrils flared; his eyes blazed. Still I dared to speak.
"Sir, your wife is alive. That is a fact you acknowledged this morning. If I lived with you as you wish, I would be your mistress. To say otherwise is clever talk—and false."

"Jane, I am not a gentle-tempered man—you forget that. I am not patient. I am not cool and dispassionate. Out of pity for me and for yourself, put your finger on my pulse, feel how it races, and—beware!"

He bared his wrist and offered it to me. The blood was draining from his cheeks and lips; they were turning ashen. I was distressed on all sides. To agitate him so deeply by the resistance he so hated was cruel. To give in was out of the question. I did what human beings do instinctively when driven to the very limit—I looked for help to one higher than man. The words "God help me!" burst involuntarily from my lips.

"I am a fool!" cried Mr. Rochester suddenly. "I keep telling her I am not married and don't explain why. I forget she knows nothing about that woman's character, or the circumstances of my infernal union with her. Oh, I am certain Jane will agree with me once she knows everything I know! Just put your hand in mine, Janet—so I may have the proof of touch as well as sight that you are near me—and I will show you in a few words the real state of the case. Can you listen to me?"
"Yes, sir; for hours if you wish."
"I ask only minutes. Jane, did you ever hear or know that I was not the eldest son of my family—that I once had an older brother?"
"I remember Mrs. Fairfax told me so once."
"And did you ever hear that my father was a greedy, grasping man?"
"I have heard something to that effect."

"Well, Jane, being so, he was determined to keep the estate intact. He could not bear the thought of dividing his property and leaving me a fair share: everything, he resolved, should go to my brother Rowland. Yet he could not stand the idea of a son of his being a poor man. I had to be provided for through a wealthy marriage. He found me a match early on. Mr. Mason, a West Indian planter and merchant, was an old acquaintance of his. My father confirmed that his wealth was real and vast; he made inquiries. Mr. Mason, he discovered, had a son and a daughter; and he learned that Mason could and would give the daughter a fortune of thirty thousand pounds. That was enough. When I left university, I was sent to Jamaica to marry a bride who had already been chosen for me. My father said nothing about her money, but he told me Miss Mason was the beauty of Spanish Town—and that was no lie. I found her a striking woman, in the style of Blanche Ingram: tall, dark, and majestic. Her family wanted to secure me because I came from good stock; and so did she. They showed her to me at parties, magnificently dressed. I rarely saw her alone and had very little private conversation with her. She flattered me and lavishly displayed her charms and accomplishments for my pleasure. Every man in her circle seemed to admire her and envy me. I was dazzled, excited. My senses were aroused; and being ignorant, inexperienced, and naive, I thought I loved her. There is no folly so absurd that the stupid rivalries of society, the recklessness and blindness of youth, will not drive a man to commit it. Her relatives encouraged me; rivals goaded me; she seduced me: a marriage was accomplished almost before I knew what had happened. Oh, I have no respect for myself when I think of that act!—an agony of inward shame overwhelms me. I never loved her, I never respected her, I did not even know her. I was not sure of a single virtue in her nature. I had seen neither modesty, nor kindness, nor honesty, nor refinement in her mind or manners—and I married her: gross, groveling, blind fool that I was! With less sin I might have—but let me remember who I am speaking to."

"My bride's mother, I had never met. I understood she was dead. The honeymoon over, I learned my mistake: she was not dead, only mad, and shut up in a lunatic asylum. There was a younger brother, too—a complete mute and imbecile. The elder one, whom you have seen (and whom I cannot hate, even while I despise all his family, because he has some grain of affection in his feeble mind, shown in his ongoing concern for his wretched sister, and also in a dog-like loyalty he once showed me)—he will probably end up in the same state one day. My father and my brother Rowland knew all this; but they thought only of the thirty thousand pounds and joined in the conspiracy against me."

"These were despicable discoveries. But except for the treachery of concealing them, I would not have made them a subject of reproach to my wife—even when I found her nature entirely alien to mine, her tastes repulsive to me, her mind common, low, narrow, and utterly incapable of being led to anything higher or expanded to anything greater. Even when I found that I could not spend a single evening, or even a single hour, with her in comfort; that no real conversation could be sustained between us, because whatever subject I raised, she immediately twisted into something coarse, trite, perverse, and stupid. Even when I discovered that I would never have a peaceful household, because no servant could endure the constant explosions of her violent and unreasonable temper, or the vexation of her absurd, contradictory, impossible orders—even then I held myself back. I avoided reproaches, I stifled complaints. I tried to swallow my regret and disgust in private. I suppressed the deep loathing I felt."

"Jane, I will not burden you with abominable details: a few strong words will convey what I have to say. I lived with that woman upstairs for four years, and before that time she had already tested me severely. Her character ripened and worsened with terrifying speed; her vices sprang up fast and rank. They were so powerful that only cruelty could check them, and I would not use cruelty. What a tiny intellect she had, and what enormous appetites! How fearful were the consequences those appetites brought upon me! Bertha Mason, the true daughter of her infamous mother, dragged me through all the hideous and degrading agonies that must attend a man bound to a wife who is both drunk and unfaithful."

"My brother had died in the interval, and at the end of the four years my father died too. I was rich enough now—yet poor to a hideous degree: a nature as gross, impure, and depraved as any I had ever encountered was joined to mine, and called by the law and by society a part of me. And I could not free myself through any legal means, because the doctors now discovered that my wife was mad—her excesses had prematurely brought out the seeds of insanity. Jane, you don't like my story; you look almost sick—shall I save the rest for another day?"
"No, sir, finish it now. I pity you—I do earnestly pity you."

"Pity, Jane, from some people is a poisonous and insulting kind of offering—the sort you are justified in hurling back in the faces of those who give it. But that is the pity born of callous, selfish hearts: a self-centered pain at hearing of suffering, mixed with ignorant contempt for those who have endured it. But that is not your pity, Jane. It is not the feeling that fills your whole face at this moment—that brims in your eyes—that heaves in your chest—that trembles through the hand you have placed in mine. Your pity, my darling, is the suffering mother of love: its anguish is the birth-pang of that divine passion. I accept it, Jane; let the child come freely—my arms are ready to receive her."
"Now, sir, go on. What did you do when you found she was mad?"

"Jane, I came to the very edge of despair. A last remnant of self-respect was all that stood between me and the abyss. In the eyes of the world, I was no doubt covered in grimy dishonor; but I resolved to be clean in my own sight—and to the end I rejected the contamination of her crimes, and wrenched myself free from any connection to her mental decay. Still, society linked my name and person with hers. I still saw her and heard her daily. Something of her breath—ugh!—mixed with the air I breathed. And besides, I remembered that I had once been her husband—a memory that was then, and remains now, unspeakably revolting to me. Moreover, I knew that while she lived, I could never be the husband of another and better wife; and, though she was five years older than me (her family and father had lied to me even about her age), she was likely to live as long as I was, being as physically robust as she was mentally broken. So at the age of twenty-six, I was without hope."

"One night I had been woken by her screaming—since the doctors had declared her mad, she had, of course, been locked up. It was a burning West Indian night, the kind that often comes before the hurricanes of those climates. Unable to sleep, I got up and opened the window. The air was like sulfur fumes—I could find no relief anywhere. Mosquitoes buzzed in and droned sullenly around the room; the sea, which I could hear from there, rumbled dully like an earthquake. Black clouds were building above it; the moon was sinking into the waves, broad and red, like a hot cannonball—it threw its last bloody light over a world trembling on the edge of a storm. I was physically affected by the atmosphere and the scene, and my ears were filled with the curses the madwoman still shrieked out—mixing my name with such demonic hatred, such language! No woman of the streets ever had a fouler vocabulary. Though she was two rooms away, I heard every word—the thin walls of the West Indian house were no barrier to her howls."

"'This life,' I said at last, 'is hell. This is the air—those are the sounds of the bottomless pit! I have a right to deliver myself from it if I can. The sufferings of this mortal existence will leave me when I shed this heavy flesh that weighs down my soul. I have no fear of the fanatic's burning eternity: there is no future state worse than this present one—let me break free, and go home to God!'"

"I said this while I knelt and unlocked a trunk containing a pair of loaded pistols: I meant to shoot myself. I entertained the thought for only a moment; for, not being insane, the crisis of pure and total despair that had given rise to the wish and plan of self-destruction passed in a second."

"A wind fresh from Europe blew across the ocean and rushed through the open window. The storm broke, streamed, thundered, blazed, and the air grew clean. I then formed and fixed a resolution. While I walked beneath the dripping orange trees of my wet garden, among its soaked pomegranates and pineapples, and while the brilliant dawn of the tropics kindled around me—I reasoned like this, Jane—and listen now, for it was true Wisdom that comforted me in that hour, and showed me the right path to follow."

"The sweet wind from Europe was still whispering in the refreshed leaves, and the Atlantic was thundering in glorious freedom. My heart, dried up and scorched for so long, swelled in response and filled with living blood. My whole being longed for renewal—my soul thirsted for a pure drink. I saw hope return—and felt regeneration was possible. From a flowering archway at the bottom of my garden, I gazed out over the sea—bluer than the sky. The old world lay beyond; bright prospects opened before me:"

"'Go,' said Hope, 'and live again in Europe: there it is not known what a stained name you carry, nor what a foul burden is chained to you. You may take the madwoman with you to England; confine her with proper care and precautions at Thornfield; then travel wherever you wish, and form whatever new bond you like. That woman, who has so abused your patience, so stained your name, so outraged your honor, so blighted your youth—she is not your wife, nor are you her husband. See that she is cared for as her condition requires, and you have done all that God and humanity ask of you. Let her identity, her connection to you, be buried in oblivion: you are not bound to reveal them to any living soul. Place her in safety and comfort: cover her degradation with secrecy, and leave her.'"

"I acted on precisely that advice. My father and brother had not made my marriage known to their acquaintances, because in the very first letter I wrote to inform them of the union—having already begun to feel extreme disgust at its consequences, and, from the family's character and constitution, seeing a hideous future opening before me—I added an urgent request to keep it secret. And very soon the infamous behavior of the wife my father had chosen for me was such as to make him ashamed to acknowledge her as his daughter-in-law. Far from wanting to announce the connection, he became as eager to conceal it as I was."

"To England, then, I brought her; a terrifying voyage I had with such a monster aboard ship. I was glad when I finally got her to Thornfield and saw her safely installed in that third-story room, whose secret inner chamber she has now, for ten years, made into a wild animal's den—a goblin's cell. I had some difficulty finding an attendant for her, since it was necessary to choose someone whose loyalty could be depended on; for her ravings would inevitably betray my secret. Besides, she had lucid intervals of days—sometimes weeks—which she spent abusing me. At last I hired Grace Poole from the Grimsby Retreat. She and the surgeon Carter (who treated Mason's wounds that night he was stabbed and savaged) are the only two I have ever trusted with my secret. Mrs. Fairfax may indeed have suspected something, but she could have had no definite knowledge of the facts. Grace has, on the whole, been a good keeper; though, partly because of a failing of her own that nothing seems to cure—an occupational hazard of her stressful profession—her vigilance has been defeated more than once. The madwoman is both cunning and vicious; she has never failed to exploit her guard's temporary lapses: once to steal the knife with which she stabbed her brother, and twice to get hold of the key to her room and escape in the night. On the first of those occasions, she tried to burn me in my bed. On the second, she made that ghastly visit to you. I thank Providence, which watched over you, that she spent her fury on your wedding clothes, which perhaps stirred vague memories of her own bridal days. But what might have happened—I cannot bear to think about. When I remember the creature that lunged at my throat this morning, its black and scarlet face hanging over the nest of my dove, my blood curdles—"
"And what, sir," I asked, as he paused, "did you do when you had settled her here? Where did you go?"

"What did I do, Jane? I turned myself into a will-o'-the-wisp. Where did I go? I pursued wanderings as wild as those of a spirit in March. I headed for the Continent, and roamed restlessly through all its lands. My single desire was to find a good and intelligent woman I could love—a contrast to the fury I had left at Thornfield—"
"But you could not marry, sir."

"I had determined and was convinced that I could and should. It was not my original intention to deceive, as I have deceived you. I meant to tell my story plainly and make my proposals openly. It seemed to me so perfectly rational that I should be considered free to love and be loved that I never doubted some woman could be found who was willing and able to understand my situation and accept me, despite the curse I carried."
"Well, sir?"

"When you are curious, Jane, you always make me smile. You open your eyes like an eager bird and shift restlessly now and then, as if words in speech don't come fast enough for you and you want to read the very heart itself. But before I go on, tell me what you mean by your 'Well, sir?' It is a little phrase you use constantly, and many a time it has drawn me on and on through endless talk. I am not sure why."
"I mean: What next? How did you proceed? What came of it?"
"Exactly! And what do you wish to know now?"
"Whether you found anyone you liked; whether you asked her to marry you; and what she said."

"I can tell you whether I found anyone I liked, and whether I asked her to marry me. But what she said is yet to be recorded in the book of Fate. For ten long years I roamed, living first in one capital, then another: sometimes in St. Petersburg, more often in Paris, occasionally in Rome, Naples, and Florence. With plenty of money and the passport of an old family name, I could choose my own company. No circles were closed to me. I looked for my ideal of a woman among English ladies, French countesses, Italian signoras, and German noblewomen. I could not find her. Sometimes, for a fleeting moment, I thought I caught a glance, heard a voice, saw a figure that promised the fulfillment of my dream—but I was soon disappointed. You are not to think I demanded perfection, either of mind or body. I longed only for what suited me—for the opposite of the Creole. And I longed in vain. Among them all I found not one whom, had I been ever so free, I—warned as I was of the risks, the horrors, the revulsion of mismatched unions—would have asked to marry me. Disappointment made me reckless. I tried pleasure-seeking—never debauchery: that I hated, and still hate. That was my wife's nature: a deep-rooted disgust at it and at her restrained me considerably, even in my pleasures. Any enjoyment that bordered on excess seemed to bring me closer to her and her vices, and I avoided it."

"Yet I could not live alone, so I tried the companionship of mistresses. The first I chose was Céline Varens—another of those steps that make a man despise himself when he looks back. You already know what she was and how my affair with her ended. She had two successors: an Italian, Giacinta, and a German, Clara; both considered remarkably beautiful. But what was their beauty to me after a few weeks? Giacinta was unprincipled and violent: I tired of her in three months. Clara was honest and quiet but dull, mindless, and incapable of depth—not at all to my taste. I was glad to give her enough money to set herself up in a good business, and so get rid of her respectably. But, Jane, I can see from your face that you are not forming a very favorable opinion of me right now. You think me an unfeeling, unprincipled rake—don't you?"

"I don't like you as well as I have at other times, sir. Did it not seem to you the least bit wrong to live that way, first with one mistress and then another? You talk of it as though it were nothing remarkable."

"It was my way of life, and I did not like it. It was a degrading form of existence: I should never want to return to it. Keeping a mistress is the next worst thing to buying a slave: both are often by nature, and always by position, inferior. And to live intimately with inferiors is degrading. I now hate the memory of the time I spent with Céline, Giacinta, and Clara."

I felt the truth of those words; and I drew from them the certain conclusion that if I were ever to forget myself and everything I had been taught—under any pretext, with any justification, through any temptation—and become the successor of those poor women, he would one day regard me with the same contempt that now, in his mind, tainted their memory. I did not voice this conviction: it was enough to feel it. I stamped it on my heart, so it might remain there to help me when the time of trial came.

"Now, Jane, why don't you say 'Well, sir?' I am not done. You look serious. You still disapprove of me, I see. But let me come to the point. Last January, free of all mistresses—in a harsh, bitter frame of mind, the result of a useless, wandering, lonely life—eaten away by disappointment, hostile toward all men, and especially toward all womankind (for I had begun to regard the notion of an intelligent, faithful, loving woman as a mere fantasy)—called back by business, I returned to England."

"On a frosty winter afternoon, I rode within sight of Thornfield Hall. Detested place! I expected no peace there—no pleasure. On a stile in Hay Lane I saw a quiet little figure sitting by itself. I passed it as carelessly as I did the pollarded willow across from it: I had no premonition of what it would be to me. No inner warning that the ruler of my life—my spirit for good or evil—waited there in humble form. I did not know it, even when, after Mesrour's accident, it came up and gravely offered to help me. Childish and slender creature! It seemed as if a sparrow had hopped to my foot and offered to carry me on its tiny wing. I was surly; but the thing would not go away: it stood beside me with a strange persistence, and looked and spoke with a sort of authority. I needed help, and from that hand: and helped I was."

"When I had once placed my weight on that frail shoulder, something new—a fresh energy and awareness—flowed into me. It was fortunate I had learned that this little creature must return to me—that it belonged to my house below—or I could not have watched it slip from under my hand and vanish behind the dim hedge without keen regret. I heard you come home that night, Jane, though probably you did not know that I thought of you or listened for you. The next day I watched you—unseen—for half an hour, while you played with Adèle in the gallery. It was a snowy day, I remember, and you could not go outdoors. I was in my room; the door was ajar: I could both listen and watch. Adèle claimed your attention for a while; yet I fancied your thoughts were elsewhere. But you were very patient with her, my little Jane; you talked to her and entertained her for a long time. When at last she left you, you immediately fell into a deep reverie. You began slowly pacing the gallery. Now and then, passing a window, you glanced out at the thick-falling snow; you listened to the moaning wind, and then you paced gently on and dreamed. I think those daydreams were not dark: there was a pleasant glow in your eye now and then, a soft excitement in your expression, that spoke not of bitter, gloomy brooding, but of the sweet musings of youth when its spirit follows Hope on willing wings up to an imagined heaven. The voice of Mrs. Fairfax, speaking to a servant in the hall, woke you; and how curiously you smiled to yourself, Janet! There was much sense in your smile: it was very shrewd, and seemed to mock your own daydreaming. It seemed to say, 'My lovely visions are all very well, but I must not forget they are completely unreal. I have a rosy sky and a green flowering paradise in my mind; but outside, I am perfectly aware, a rough road lies at my feet, and dark storms are gathering around me.' You ran downstairs and asked Mrs. Fairfax for some task: the weekly household accounts to go over, or something like that, I believe. I was annoyed with you for disappearing from my sight."

"I waited impatiently for evening, when I could summon you to me. An unusual—to me, an entirely new—character I suspected was yours: I wanted to explore it deeper and know it better. You entered the room with a look and manner at once shy and independent. You were quaintly dressed—much as you are now. I made you talk; before long I found you full of strange contrasts. Your dress and manner were governed by rules; your air was often uncertain, altogether that of someone refined by nature but completely unused to society, and somewhat afraid of making herself conspicuous through some blunder. Yet when spoken to, you raised a keen, daring, and glowing eye to your questioner's face: there was perception and power in every glance you gave; when pressed with close questions, you gave ready and direct answers. Very quickly you seemed to grow comfortable with me. I believe you felt the bond between you and your grim, cross master, Jane; for it was remarkable to see how quickly a certain easy confidence settled your manner. Growl as I might, you showed no surprise, fear, annoyance, or displeasure at my moodiness. You watched me, and now and then smiled at me with a simple yet knowing grace I cannot describe. I was at once satisfied and stimulated by what I saw: I liked what I had found and wanted to see more. Yet for a long time I kept my distance and rarely sought your company. I was an intellectual connoisseur, and wished to prolong the pleasure of this novel and intriguing acquaintance. Besides, I was troubled for a while by a fear that if I handled the flower too freely, its bloom would fade—the sweet charm of freshness would leave it. I did not then know that it was no passing blossom, but the radiant likeness of one, cut in an indestructible gem. Moreover, I wanted to see whether you would seek me out if I avoided you—but you did not. You stayed in the schoolroom as still as your own desk and easel; if by chance I met you, you passed me as quickly and with as little recognition as respect would allow. Your usual expression in those days, Jane, was thoughtful: not despondent, for you were not sickly; but not cheerful either, for you had little hope and no real pleasure. I wondered what you thought of me—or if you ever thought of me—and resolved to find out."

"I paid you more attention. There was something glad in your look and warm in your manner when you talked. I saw you had a social heart; it was the silent schoolroom—the tedium of your life—that made you melancholy. I allowed myself the pleasure of being kind to you; kindness stirred emotion quickly. Your face grew soft, your voice gentle. I liked hearing my name spoken by your lips in a grateful, happy tone. I used to enjoy a chance meeting with you, Jane, in those days. There was a charming hesitation in your manner: you glanced at me with a slight unease—a hovering doubt. You did not know what my mood might be—whether I would play the master and be stern, or the friend and be warm. I was now too fond of you to often pretend the first; and when I extended my hand warmly, such color and light and joy rose in your young, hopeful face that I could barely keep myself from pulling you right then and there to my heart."

"Don't speak any more of those days, sir," I interrupted, secretly wiping tears from my eyes. His words were torture to me; for I knew what I must do—and do soon—and all these memories, all these revelations of his feelings, only made my task harder.
"No, Jane," he replied. "Why dwell on the Past when the Present is so much more certain—the Future so much brighter?"
I shuddered to hear that deluded claim.

"You see now how things stand—do you not?" he continued. "After a youth and manhood spent half in unspeakable misery and half in dreary solitude, I have for the first time found what I can truly love—I have found you. You are my kindred spirit—my better self—my good angel. I am bound to you with a powerful attachment. I think you good, gifted, and lovely: a deep, solemn passion has taken hold of my heart. It draws me to you, wraps my existence around you, and, burning in a pure, powerful flame, fuses you and me into one."

"It was because I felt and knew this that I resolved to marry you. To tell me I already had a wife is meaningless: you know now that I had only a hideous demon. I was wrong to try to deceive you; but I feared a stubbornness in your character. I feared deeply ingrained principles. I wanted to have you safe before risking any confessions. This was cowardly: I should have appealed to your nobility and generosity from the start, as I do now—opened to you plainly my life of agony—described my hunger and thirst for a higher and worthier existence—shown you not my resolution (that word is too weak), but my irresistible drive to love faithfully and well, where I am faithfully and well loved in return. Then I should have asked you to accept my pledge of faithfulness and give me yours. Jane—give it to me now."
A pause.
"Why are you silent, Jane?"

I was being tested as if by fire: a hand of red-hot iron gripped my insides. Terrible moment: full of struggle, darkness, burning! No human being who ever lived could wish to be loved more than I was loved; and the man who loved me so, I absolutely worshipped. And I had to renounce both love and idol. One grim word summed up my unbearable duty—"Go!"
"Jane, you understand what I want from you? Just this promise: 'I will be yours, Mr. Rochester.'"
"Mr. Rochester, I will not be yours."
Another long silence.

"Jane!" he began again, with a gentleness that broke me with grief and turned me stone-cold with ominous terror—for this quiet voice was the panting of a lion rising. "Jane, do you mean to go one way in the world, and let me go another?"
"I do."
"Jane" (bending toward me and embracing me), "do you mean it now?"
"I do."
"And now?" softly kissing my forehead and cheek.
"I do," pulling myself free from his hold, quickly and completely.
"Oh, Jane, this is bitter! This—this is wicked. It would not be wicked to love me."
"It would be wicked to obey you."
A wild look crossed his brow—flashed over his features: he rose; but he held back still. I placed my hand on the back of a chair for support. I shook, I was afraid—but I was resolved.

"One moment, Jane. Look at the horrible life that awaits me when you are gone. All happiness will be ripped away with you. What is left then? For a wife I have only the madwoman upstairs: you might as well point me to a corpse in the churchyard. What shall I do, Jane? Where shall I turn for a companion and for some hope?"
"Do as I do: trust in God and in yourself. Believe in heaven. Hope to meet again there."
"Then you will not give in?"
"No."
"Then you condemn me to live in misery and die accursed?" His voice rose.
"I advise you to live without sin, and I wish you to die at peace."
"Then you snatch love and innocence from me? You fling me back on lust for a passion—vice for an occupation?"
"Mr. Rochester, I no more assign that fate to you than I reach for it myself. We were born to struggle and endure—you as well as I. Do so. You will forget me before I forget you."

"You make me a liar with such words. You insult my honor. I declared I could not change: you tell me to my face I shall change soon. And what a distortion of judgment, what a perversity in your ideas, is proven by your behavior! Is it better to drive a fellow creature to despair than to break a mere human law—no man being injured by the breach? For you have neither relatives nor acquaintances whom you need fear to offend by living with me."

This was true. And while he spoke, my very conscience and reason turned traitor against me and accused me of a crime in resisting him. They spoke almost as loudly as Feeling: and Feeling clamored wildly. "Oh, give in!" it said. "Think of his misery; think of his danger—look at the state he will be in when left alone; remember his reckless nature; think about what desperate acts might follow on your refusal—soothe him; save him; love him; tell him you love him and will be his. Who in the world cares for you? or who will be hurt by what you do?"

Still, the answer was unyielding—"I care for myself. The more alone, the more friendless, the more without support I am, the more I will respect myself. I will keep the law given by God, sanctioned by man. I will hold to the principles I received when I was sane, not mad—as I am now. Laws and principles are not for the times when there is no temptation: they are for moments like this, when body and soul rise up against their authority. Firm they stand; and I shall not break them. If at my individual convenience I might break them, what would they be worth? They have worth—so I have always believed; and if I cannot believe it now, it is because I am out of my mind, with my blood on fire and my veins churning. I have a prior resolution—that resolution shall stand."

I did stand by it. Mr. Rochester, reading my face, saw that I had. His fury reached its peak: he had to yield to it for a moment, whatever came next. He crossed the floor and seized my arm and gripped my waist. He seemed to devour me with his blazing gaze: physically, at that moment, I felt powerless as a reed. But mentally I felt as if I stood somewhere beyond his grasp, above his reach—an essence that neither his fury nor his despair could touch. I looked at his face—and a strange energy ran through me. He had already released my waist and had only my arm—I moved to free myself from that too.

"Never," said he through clenched teeth, "never was anything at once so fragile and so unconquerable. She feels like a mere reed in my hand!" (And he shook me with the force of his grip.) "I could bend her with my finger and thumb: and what good would it do if I bent, if I tore up, if I crushed her? Think about this, conscience—and think about the effect on yourself, passion. Think about it—consider it—think about her eye, her face: think about what she is. Look at the look in those eyes. How soft and full of feeling they are! How they still shine with a gentle glow—a glow of devotion and grief for me! Look at the sweet lines of that mouth!" (I was startled, because these last words were said as if to a vision, something unseen by me but apparently visible to him.) "I could bend her" (his voice was tortured), "but would she bend? Would she yield willingly? No—even if I tried, I’d find only tow and splinter in my hands. Forced compliance would give me only what? Only this small frame—this pale face, these delicate features. And the soul? Her soul would escape from my grip like a caged skylark launching upward through shattered bars into the clouds."

As he said this, he released me from his grasp and only looked at me. The look was far harder to resist than his frenzied hold. Only a fool, however, would have given in now. I had faced down and baffled his fury; now I had to escape his sorrow. I moved toward the door.
"You are going, Jane?"
"I am going, sir."
"You are leaving me?"
"Yes."
"You will not come? You will not be my comfort, my rescuer? My deep love, my wild grief, my desperate prayer—they are nothing to you?"
What indescribable anguish was in his voice! How hard it was to repeat firmly, "I am going."
"Jane!"
"Mr. Rochester!"
"Then go—I consent. But remember, you leave me here in agony. Go to your room. Think over everything I have said. And, Jane, spare a thought for my suffering—think of me."
He turned away. He threw himself facedown on the sofa. "Oh, Jane! My hope—my love—my life!" broke in anguish from his lips. Then came a deep, wrenching sob.

I had already reached the door; but, reader, I walked back—walked back as determinedly as I had retreated. I knelt beside him. I turned his face from the cushion toward me. I kissed his cheek. I smoothed his hair with my hand.
"God bless you, my dear master!" I said. "God keep you from harm and wrong—direct you, comfort you—reward you well for your past kindness to me."
"Little Jane's love would have been my best reward," he answered. "Without it, my heart is broken. But Jane will give me her love: yes—nobly, generously."
The blood rushed to his face; fire flashed from his eyes; he sprang upright; he held his arms out; but I dodged the embrace, and instantly left the room.
"Farewell!" was the cry of my heart as I left him. Despair added, "Farewell forever!"

That night I never expected to sleep; but a slumber fell on me as soon as I lay down. I was carried back in my dreams to childhood: I dreamt I lay in the red room at Gateshead; that the night was dark, and my mind filled with strange fears. The light that long ago had terrified me flashed on the wall. The ghost-like figure of a gleaming moon rose into the sky. I watched it with the panic of a child. As it climbed the dark ceiling and took shape, it spoke to my spirit—unutterably far away, yet so close, whispering through my heart—
"My daughter, flee temptation."
"Mother, I will."

So I answered after I had woken from the trancelike dream. It was still night, but July nights are short: soon after midnight, dawn comes. "It cannot be too early to start the task I must complete," I thought. I rose. I was dressed; for I had taken off nothing but my shoes. I knew where to find a small silk purse in my drawer: it held twenty shillings—my entire fortune. I picked up my straw bonnet and pinned on my shawl. I took the purse and my slippers, which I would put on later, and stole silently from my room.

"Farewell, kind Mrs. Fairfax!" I whispered as I slipped past her door. "Farewell, my darling Adèle!" I said as I glanced toward the nursery. There was no thought of going in to embrace her. I had to get past a sharp ear: for all I knew, it might be listening even now.

I would have passed Mr. Rochester's room without stopping; but my heart, momentarily halting its beat at that threshold, forced my feet to stop as well. No sleep was there: the man inside was pacing restlessly from wall to wall; and again and again he sighed as I listened. There was a heaven—a temporary heaven—in this room for me, if I chose. I only had to go in and say—
"Mr. Rochester, I will love you and live with you through life until death," and a fountain of joy would spring to my lips. I thought of this.

That kind master, who could not sleep now, was waiting impatiently for morning. He would send for me in the morning; I would be gone. He would have me searched for: in vain. He would feel himself abandoned; his love rejected. He would suffer; perhaps grow desperate. I thought of this too. My hand moved toward the lock. I stopped myself. I forced myself away. I crept on.

In a daze I made my way downstairs. I knew what I had to do, and I did it mechanically. I found the key to the side door in the kitchen. I also found a small bottle of oil and a feather. I oiled the key and the lock. I got some water; I got some bread: for I might have to walk far, and my strength, severely tested in the last day, must not fail me completely. I opened the door, stepped through it, and closed it softly. Dim dawn glimmered in the yard. The gate, too, stood open. I slipped through and was gone.

A mile off, beyond the fields, lay a road that led in the opposite direction from Millcote; a road I had never traveled but often noticed, wondering where it went. That was where I headed now. No reflection was allowed: not a single glance back, not even one forward. Not one thought of the future could be permitted. The first thing to be done was to move past the moors and beyond the reach of anyone from Thornfield.

I skirted fields and hedges and lanes until after sunrise. I believe it was a lovely summer morning: I know my shoes, which I had put on as I left the house, were soon wet with dew. But I looked neither at the rising sun, nor the smiling sky, nor the awakening countryside. A condemned prisoner being led to the scaffold thinks not of the flowers that line the road, but of the block and axe at its end—or rather of the grave that waits beyond. I thought of a drain deep and dark through which a torrent of blood was pouring, from which no dam could stop the flow.

When I got there, I was forced to stop and rest under the hedge; and while I sat, I heard wheels and saw a coach approaching. I stood and raised my hand; it stopped. I asked where it was going: the driver named a place far away, where I was sure Mr. Rochester had no connections. I asked the fare: he said thirty shillings. I counted out my purse. It came to twenty. I told him I could pay only that much. He said he would take me for that. I got in—the coach drove on.

Gentle reader, may you never feel what I felt then! May your eyes never shed such stormy, scalding, heart-wrung tears as poured from mine. May you never appeal to Heaven in prayers so hopeless and so agonized as left my lips in that hour; for never may you, like me, dread to be the instrument of evil to the one you wholly love.
